note: Each biweekly cycle, generate_report.py's web search also produces a private-company landscape per layer -- an overview plus companies grouped by technology sub-category -- and merges new companies in automatically (see update_private_markets()). Merge is additive and never touches a company once it's diligenced: true -- flip that flag once a row reflects real internal diligence, and the automation will leave it alone from then on. The overview paragraph itself refreshes every cycle since it's a categorical summary, not a specific company's diligence.

energy.overview: The private energy landscape splits into two bets on very different timelines: fusion and advanced-fission developers racing toward first commercial power by the late 2020s, and storage/geothermal companies solving the nearer-term problem of firming renewables already on the grid. None of the frontier reactor bets have delivered commercial power yet -- the category is still pre-revenue at scale.

companies.notes: Fusion energy developer building the SPARC tokamak; spun out of MIT, backed by Breakthrough Energy Ventures among others.
Fusion energy developer with a power purchase agreement targeting 50MW of fusion power for Microsoft.
Advanced nuclear reactor developer (Natrium design) founded by Bill Gates.
Molten-salt-cooled small modular reactor developer with a Google power purchase agreement.
Iron-air battery maker targeting multi-day, grid-scale energy storage.
Enhanced geothermal energy developer supplying firm, round-the-clock clean power.

cooling.overview: Private cooling companies split cleanly by approach: immersion specialists betting that fully submerging hardware is the endpoint for extreme-density racks, and direct-to-chip developers betting that retrofittable, waterless cold-plate designs win on cost and compatibility with existing air-cooled facilities.

companies.notes: Immersion cooling systems for data centers, expanding into owning its own AI data center capacity.
Two-phase and single-phase immersion cooling technology for high-density AI racks.
Precision, chassis-level liquid cooling for data center and edge deployments.
Waterless, two-phase direct-to-chip liquid cooling technology.
Two-phase direct-to-chip cooling systems designed to retrofit existing air-cooled data centers.

power.overview: The private power landscape here is mostly software, not hardware: demand-forecasting and grid-flexibility platforms are trying to squeeze more usable capacity out of an interconnection-constrained grid faster than new physical capacity like transformers and storage can be built.

companies.notes: AI-driven electricity demand forecasting for grid operators and large power consumers.
Software that lets data centers flex power consumption to ease grid interconnection bottlenecks.
Behind-the-meter power management aimed at faster-to-deploy, flexible data center capacity.
Long-duration metal-hydrogen battery storage for grid and industrial backup power.

silicon.overview: Private companies barely register at the leading edge of fabs and memory -- this category is structurally dominated by public incumbents (TSMC, Samsung, Micron, SK Hynix). Rapidus is the one credible independent bet, a government-and-consortium-backed attempt to rebuild Japan's domestic foundry capacity.

companies.notes: Japanese foundry consortium backed by Toyota, Sony, NTT, and the Japanese government, building a 2nm fab to re-establish domestic leading-edge chip manufacturing.

compute.overview: The private compute landscape is the most crowded in the value chain: inference-specialized chip startups are betting speed and cost beat general-purpose GPUs for serving models, while wafer-scale and reconfigurable-architecture players are betting on training and flexibility instead. Several have flirted with public listings without completing one.

companies.notes: Purpose-built LPU (language processing unit) chips for ultra-fast, low-latency AI inference.
In-memory computing AI inference chips optimized for datacenter deployment.
AI chip startup building transformer-specific ASICs (the 'Sohu' chip).
Wafer-scale AI training/inference systems (CS-3/CS-4); has previously filed for and withdrawn a public listing.
RISC-V-based AI accelerator company led by chip designer Jim Keller.
Reconfigurable dataflow AI chips and a full-stack enterprise AI platform.

networking.overview: Private networking companies are almost entirely optical-interconnect plays betting that co-packaged optics displaces pluggable transceivers at the rack level, plus networking-silicon startups pushing to keep pace with GPU cluster bandwidth demands.

companies.notes: Optical I/O chiplets for high-bandwidth, low-power AI cluster interconnect.
Photonic computing and optical interconnect technology for AI data centers.
Networking silicon designed to scale GPU cluster interconnect bandwidth.

serversdc.overview: The private data center landscape splits into large, PE-and-infrastructure-backed developers building at hyperscale, and a newer cohort pairing data center development directly with unconventional, often stranded, power sources.

companies.notes: Hyperscale data center developer and operator, backed by DigitalBridge.
Data center developer and operator backed by Macquarie Asset Management.
Data center developer building modular, hyperscale-ready campuses.
Data center developer and operator backed by IPI Partners.
AI-focused data center developer, notable for co-locating compute with stranded or flared energy sources.

cloud.overview: Private AI cloud providers are all reselling or optimizing access to GPU capacity, differentiated mainly by whether they compete on raw compute access, inference-serving performance, or open-model hosting.

companies.notes: AI cloud and GPU infrastructure provider, reportedly pursuing further pre-IPO fundraising.
GPU cloud infrastructure provider.
AI cloud platform providing inference and fine-tuning infrastructure for open models.
Inference cloud platform optimized for serving open-weight and custom models.

applications.overview: The private applications landscape has two tiers: frontier labs racing on raw model capability and compute access, and vertical or consumer application companies racing to build defensible products on top of those models before capability gaps close.
